For context, from https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/10845#issuecomment-2577509473:

> - pytest does assertion rewriting for *everything* (even third-party modules outside of the test `rootdir`) if `python_files = *.py` is set. IMHO that is a pytest bug, though I never really was deeply involved with the assertion rewriting code, so I'd love to hear what other maintainers think.

I was able to reproduce the current behavior using a minimal pytester-based test.

When python_files = *.py is set, assertion rewriting is applied not only to collected test modules but also to non-test, locally imported modules.

I added a small repro where an external module (extmod.py) is imported by a test, and its assert is rewritten, producing the detailed assertion output (assert 10 == 42).

This seems to come from _should_rewrite relying primarily on python_files patterns, without distinguishing between collected test files and other imported modules.

I have a passing test that documents this current behavior. Happy to adjust expectations or explore design options if this is considered unintended.

We stumbled upon the same issue in Airflow - we have a way to make selective checks (based on what has changed in the incoming commit we select folders to run tests on (but we want to recursively search them). 

In some cases the selective checks resulted in (roughly):

```
pytest tests/providers tests/providers/amazon tests/providers/google
```


In pytest 7.*  that collected all `tests/providers` tests recursively (including many other subfolders of `tests/providers` - including amazon, google tests recursively as well). However with Pytest 8.3.2 that we have currently this only collects "amazon" and "google".

I downgraded pytest and checked that (as expected) the behaviour changed in Pytest 8.0.0.

I workarounded it in https://github.com/apache/airflow/pull/41499 - (I remove provider subfolders from the list) when I see I have the parent "tests/providers" also added), however, I think that behaviour is a bit unexpected - I guess it is a side effect of one of the changes in  https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/changelog.html#collection-changes, but it might be pretty disruptive if somoene had similar case - because it does not give an indication that only a subset of tests are run.

Possibly restoring old behaviour should be considered if possible.

@Famlam Yes, I can see why it might happen. The code in pytest 9.0 runs a simple syntactic dedup algorithm on the arguments, so given `. plugins plugins/tests modules analysers` it sees all the other args are nested under `.` so just removes them and keeps only `.`. The algorithm does not consider `norecursedirs`. TBH I didn't think about that.

Do you mind explaining a bit why you setup things this way? It is unusual so I'd like to understand.

Considering `norecursedir` in the algorithm is not difficult, I did it in a WIP patch here: https://github.com/bluetech/pytest/commits/collect-args-norecursedirs/. 

Even with this patch there is still a problem though, the other way around -- now tests are collected multiple times.  Might be possible to fix as well with more tinkering (what's causing it are the `session.isinitpath` checks).

> Do you mind explaining a bit why you setup things this way? It is unusual so I'd like to understand.

Apologies for the late reply! We have tests included [in the root script (under `.`)](https://github.com/osmose-qa/osmose-backend/blob/dev/osmose_config.py#L2165-L2205), as well as in the subfolders ([example](https://github.com/osmose-qa/osmose-backend/blob/dev/plugins/TagFix_Maxspeed.py#L137)). However, we also have several directories such as `.\plugins\disabled` or `[...]\generated` which shouldn't be tested. Based on the available configuration options, the most logical way to set this up (without having a very long list of exclusions) would be to use this short inclusion list and a global stop on recursion.

Removing `norecursedirs=*` altogether or setting it to some value like `disabled generated` for some reason results in an `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.` without any tests ran (not even in the main directory), using v9.0.2

Not really anything we can do without more information (as in, ideally a reproducer).

Perhaps you could help by finding the offending commit that broke things, though no guarantee that anyone will be able to fix anything only based on that either. But it'd be better than nothing at least.

To do so:

- Clone the pytest repository
- Inside your project, do a `pip install -e /path/to/pytest`
- Run your tests, they should fail
- In the pytest repository, do a `git bisect start` and `git bisect bad`
- Also there, do `git checkout 7.4.4`
- Verify that running your tests works now
- Back in the pytest repo, do `git bisect good`
- git will now check out the middle of the two versions
- In your project repo, run your tests
- In the pytest repo, depending on the outcome, do `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`
- Repeat until git tells you the culprit

See [Git - git-bisect Documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect).

Blocking a conftest is structurally impossible in various ways

Using setblocked is an absolute footgun for conftests 

I suspect a validation for that was never added because the initial implementer couldn't conceive of someone using it with a conftest 

We should error early on that

Pytest shows a order invariant difference between 2 dicts as dict equality doesn't require the order of items in a dictionary to match 

Its not clear what you sre asking for

So the request is for the display order to orient on the insert order 


Based on the code it might be a mistake that the full diff is printed 

In any case we need a deep diff to correctly implement this .

Currently pformat is used to get diff compatible left/right 

Unless a correct deep diff we can apply here is avaliable im against implementing this in pytest

@RonnyPfannschmidt [pformat](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pprint.html#pprint.pformat) has an option sort_dicts which defaults to True. It is described as "If True, dictionaries will be formatted with their keys sorted, otherwise they will be displayed in insertion order" 

Is that what is sorting the keys alphabetically in the pytest output?

If not, I found a deep diff library called deepdiff. For the example above, it gives:
```
pprint(DeepDiff(a,b))
{'dictionary_item_removed': ["root['b']", "root['a']"]}
```

> Is that what is sorting the keys alphabetically in the pytest output?

`pformat` is used here:

https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/9e9633de9da7a9fab03b4bba3a326bf85b412050/src/_pytest/assertion/util.py#L498-L541

Looks like it would be just a matter of passing `sort_dicts=False` to those `pformat` calls.

We will have to ensure compatible dict ordering in nested structures to ensure minimal diffs 

Order matching dicts in modern python make this easier but its still a caveat
